prime.problem: Two correct programs can share almost no text, and a wrong one can differ from the answer key by one character. Any grade based on resemblance to a reference will reward the wrong one.
prime.fits: The definition everything else in the deck rests on: pass@k counts samples that are correct in this sense, HumanEval supplies the tests, and the sandbox makes running them safe.
expect: exact match and BLEU as the rejected alternatives
Figure 8: correct and wrong samples overlap in BLEU
the test suite as the weak point
prime.goal: Explain why 'passes the tests' replaces 'looks like the reference', and name exactly what that grading still can't see.

attend: In the has_dup example, why does sample B get thrown away by exact match but kept by tests?
What does sample C's near-total token overlap reveal about any similarity-based grade?
If correctness is decided by tests, what happens to a sample that deletes the functionality the tests don't cover?
Why does functional correctness make 'sample 100 times and keep a passing one' a meaningful strategy at all?

must: Many programs compute the same function → a reference is just one of them → similarity to it rewards copying, not correctness → run the code on tests instead
A one-character change (!= → ==) can invert behaviour while keeping near-total overlap → text metrics rank a wrong sample above a correct different algorithm → only execution sees the flip
Correctness = passing these tests → weak or narrow suites let wrong programs pass (Qi et al.: repairs that delete functionality) → the metric is only as strong as its tests
Tests check input/output behaviour only → efficiency, readability and security stay invisible → APPS needs a separate timeout column, and insecure crypto can still pass
elevated: Grading by execution means running untrusted code → it requires a sandbox and trusted tests → cost and safety move from the grader's judgement to infrastructure
reference: Ren et al. (2020) on BLEU missing code semantics
HumanEval's 7.7 tests per problem on average
Qi et al. (2015) on weak program-repair suites

compress.prompt: From memory, rank the three has_dup samples under text similarity and under tests, and write two sentences explaining why the rankings disagree and which one the paper trusts.
checklist: similarity ranks A > C > B; tests rank A = B > C
B is a different correct algorithm; C flips one operator
text overlap measures resemblance, not behaviour
tests are the criterion developers actually use
caveat: only as good as the tests, and blind to speed and security

retrieve.q: Explain why exact match against a reference can't work as a metric for code, even in principle.
answer: infinitely many programs implement the same function
exact match scores every correct non-reference program as zero

retrieve.q: Trace what the grader does with sample C: which step reveals it is wrong, and why doesn't anything before that step?
answer: token comparison sees near-total overlap and scores it high
execution runs len(set(xs)) == len(xs) on the tests
it returns the opposite boolean, so it fails the tests

retrieve.q: You're choosing between functional correctness and human judging for a new code-generation task. What do you give up with each?
answer: tests: need trusted suites and a sandbox; blind to style, speed and security
the paper used humans only where no tests exist (Codex-D docstrings)

compare.q: BLEU and functional correctness both grade the same samples. What does each actually observe about a program, and which failure is each blind to?
answer: BLEU observes n-gram overlap with one reference; tests observe outputs on chosen inputs
BLEU is blind to behaviour-flipping small edits and to correct rewrites
tests are blind to untested inputs and to non-functional qualities

compare.q: EvalPlus keeps functional correctness but changes how the tests are produced. Which weakness named on this card does differential testing attack, and what does it still rely on?
answer: attacks weak, hand-written suites by generating many more inputs
compares outputs to the ground-truth solution
still relies on the ground truth being right

predict.q: A sample for has_dup returns True for every input. HumanEval-style tests for this problem happen to include only lists that contain duplicates. Does the sample count as correct, and what does that do to pass@k? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: It counts as correct: it passes every test it's given. pass@k goes up for a program that's plainly wrong, which is exactly the Qi et al. failure. Functional correctness moves the question from 'does it look right' to 'are the tests good enough', which is the gap EvalPlus later fills.

apply.task: Break the grader. First try to find one input on which sample C and the has_dup reference agree, and explain why there is none. Then write the smallest test set that separates C from the reference, and one extra wrong sample of your own that still passes that set.
apply.done: You explain that C is the exact negation of the reference, so any single test separates them; you give one test (e.g. [1,1] → True); and your extra wrong sample passes that test but fails an input you can name.
apply.hint: A sample that returns len(xs) > 1 passes [1,1] → True but fails [1,2].

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether the always-True sample counts as correct?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why BLEU ranks C above B?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: tests → correctness, or test quality → pass@k inflation?
What would you check first about a benchmark before trusting its pass@k?
